paragraphs: A language model’s confidence is useful only when it tracks how often its answers are correct. CaliDist examines an additional clue: whether the model remains stable when irrelevant or misleading information enters the prompt. The authors argue that confidence should account for this behavioral robustness, rather than relying only on the model’s initial score.

The method operates after prediction by introducing semantic distractors and measuring changes in both predictions and uncertainty. It uses those changes to adjust the original confidence score, penalizing susceptibility to distraction. This makes the calibration signal depend on observed behavior under altered inputs, connecting reported certainty to how easily the model’s judgment can be disturbed.

Across seven language-understanding classification benchmarks and six language models, CaliDist achieves lower Expected Calibration Error and Brier Score than strong baselines. Average calibration error falls from 23% to 7%, reported as a 70% relative improvement. These results support behavioral stability as a useful calibration signal in the evaluated classification settings.
icml-2026-calidist-calibrating-large-lan.tldr: CaliDist improves confidence calibration by measuring how strongly distractions change a model’s predictions and uncertainty.

paragraphs: A robot can develop faults after its control policy has finished training, when collecting new experience or identifying the changed system may be impractical. This paper adds an adaptive corrective controller to a frozen reinforcement learning policy. The extra controller produces residual actions that compensate for disturbances while leaving the original policy parameters unchanged during inference-time recovery.

The design borrows several principles from the cerebellum. Fixed feature expansion separates input patterns, parallel pathways provide localized corrections, and error-driven updates operate through excitatory and inhibitory eligibility traces at different time scales. A performance-based mechanism conservatively regulates correction strength and learning, helping preserve normal behavior and suppress intervention when it is unnecessary.

Experiments test actuator, dynamics, and environmental disturbances in MuJoCo. Under moderate faults, reported improvements reach 66% on HalfCheetah-v5 and 53% on Humanoid-v5, with graceful degradation under more severe shifts. The authors also find complementary robustness from consolidating persistent corrections into policy parameters, connecting immediate adaptation with longer-term changes to the controller.
icml-2026-cerebellar-inspired-residual-c.tldr: A cerebellum-inspired corrective controller helps frozen robot policies recover from faults through localized online adaptation.

paragraphs: Compute as Teacher asks how a model can improve when post-training has no ground-truth answers. Its answer is to turn multiple generated responses into a training signal. Parallel rollouts are aggregated into an estimated reference, which then supports reinforcement learning, including in domains where a program cannot directly check whether an answer is correct.

The framework separates reference estimation from reward construction. The authors explore an aggregation method called synthesis, while allowing other aggregators. For non-verifiable tasks, the estimated reference generates binary evaluation criteria called self-proposed rubrics. A language-model judge scores these auditable criteria to produce rewards, giving training a structured target derived from the model’s own inference compute.

On HealthBench, trained models match or exceed inference-time aggregation quality with nine times less test-time compute. They also compete with training from physician annotations, with improvements of up to 30% relative to the initial policy. In a verifiable setting, the framework matches leading baselines on MATH-500 in test-time reinforcement learning, supporting its applicability across both reward settings.
icml-2026-compute-as-teacher-turning-inf.tldr: Compute as Teacher converts aggregated model responses into reinforcement learning supervision, reducing the inference compute needed for strong answers.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether transformers can recognize strings that obey context-free grammars, a formal model of syntax. Under standard complexity conjectures, standard transformers cannot recognize all context-free languages, or even all regular languages. Earlier work showed that repeating transformer layers logarithmically with input length enables regular-language recognition, leaving the context-free case unresolved.

The authors construct looped transformers that recognize every context-free language using O(log N) looping layers and O(N^6) padding symbols for input length N. This is a sufficient construction: it establishes what the architecture can express with those resources. The padding requirement also creates a potentially impractical training and inference burden, despite the modest number of layer repetitions.

For natural subclasses such as unambiguous context-free languages, the authors reduce the padding requirement to O(N^3). Experiments also find that looped, padded transformers recognize context-free languages better than fixed-depth transformers. Together, the results show how architectural repetition and additional sequence space support syntax recognition, while demonstrating that restrictions on the grammar can make the construction more tractable.
icml-2026-context-free-recognition-with-.tldr: Looped transformers can recognize all context-free languages with sufficient padding, with smaller padding requirements for subclasses such as unambiguous languages.

paragraphs: Sparse tangent portfolio optimization seeks a portfolio containing few assets while targeting the tangency direction of the mean-variance frontier. The limited asset count supports interpretability, but the corresponding discrete optimization is NP-hard. A separate difficulty arises when predictions are trained for forecast accuracy: better forecasts need not translate into better portfolio decisions.

The paper connects prediction, asset selection, and portfolio re-optimization in one trainable system. It reformulates Sharpe ratio maximization as a convex programming layer compatible with Disciplined Parametrized Programming. A smooth top-k operator replaces discrete selection while enforcing exactly k selected assets. These components let gradients pass through the decision process so the predictive model can learn directly from portfolio performance.

Across four major equity markets, the approach obtains competitive and often better out-of-sample Sharpe ratios than historical and prediction-focused baselines. Gains are particularly strong when choosing among larger asset universes. The stated findings support aligning the training objective with the eventual portfolio decision, while retaining explicit control over how many assets the portfolio contains.
icml-2026-decision-focused-sparse-tangen.tldr: An end-to-end portfolio model learns predictions and exact-size asset selections directly for downstream Sharpe ratio performance.

paragraphs: DiscoForcing addresses character motion that must respond to audio as it arrives. The setting requires strictly causal processing, bounded latency, and coherent full-body movement at interactive rates. Abrupt tempo changes, drops, or user edits make this harder because previously useful audio history can become unreliable. Systems designed around complete audio sequences can degrade under these streaming conditions.

The framework combines a causal music encoder with a diffusion-forcing sequence model. The encoder captures rhythm and phase dynamics, while the sequence model trains with different noise levels across its temporal horizon. A hybrid temporal schedule and history-guided sampler manage the tradeoff between reacting quickly to new audio and maintaining consistency over extended motion sequences.

The authors implement an end-to-end interactive system with online avatar playback and humanoid deployment workflows. Under matched causality and latency constraints, DiscoForcing produces more stable long rollouts and tighter audio–motion alignment than prior baselines while retaining real-time throughput. The contribution therefore includes both a streaming generation method and evidence that its responsiveness–consistency tradeoff works under the stated deployment constraints.
icml-2026-discoforcing-a-unified-framewo.tldr: DiscoForcing generates real-time audio-responsive motion by balancing rapid adaptation to changing audio with long-term movement consistency.

paragraphs: Scientific and engineering generation tasks often require samples to obey physical, geometric, or safety constraints. This paper develops diffusion models for nonconvex feasible sets with both equality and inequality constraints. The framework enforces these restrictions throughout the diffusion process, addressing the problem of keeping intermediate states feasible as well as producing acceptable final samples.

Its central mechanism, called landing, replaces projections onto the feasible set. Such projections can be expensive or ill-defined; landing maintains feasibility without iterative Newton solves or projection failures. The framework supports both overdamped and underdamped dynamics in forward and backward sampling. Underdamped dynamics accelerate movement toward the prior distribution, reducing the simulation burden associated with constrained diffusion.

On benchmarks containing equality constraints and mixtures of constraint types, the approach matches the sample quality of state-of-the-art baselines while substantially reducing computational cost. The authors report fewer function evaluations and lower memory use during training and inference. These findings suggest that the way feasibility is maintained can materially affect efficiency without requiring a loss of sample quality in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-efficient-diffusion-models-und.tldr: A landing mechanism makes constrained diffusion more efficient while maintaining feasibility under nonconvex equality and inequality constraints.

paragraphs: Many scheduling problems repeatedly choose one item from a set of candidates. A priority rule makes this decision by scoring candidates and selecting the highest-ranked one. The Factorized Scheduling Principle framework aims to learn such rules while keeping their structure interpretable and allowing them to transfer between systems of different sizes.

The framework describes system states through condition distributions. It then expresses the scheduling principle as a sum of components involving individual conditions and pairs of conditions, subject to identifiability constraints. This decomposition exposes separate contributions and interactions instead of placing the entire decision inside an undivided function. Deployment still uses a simple priority-based decision structure.

Training combines a policy-based objective with a temporal-difference signal defined over the condition distribution. Experiments on synthetic and realistic scheduling tasks report strong performance, interpretability, and zero-shot generalization across system scales. The findings support learning a structured scheduling rule whose components remain inspectable and whose usefulness can extend to differently sized systems without additional training.
icml-2026-factorized-scheduling-principl.tldr: Factorized Scheduling Principle learns interpretable priority rules that show zero-shot transfer across different system sizes.

paragraphs: Large set cover problems can contain millions of variables, making rapid optimization difficult. Breaking them into bounded subproblems helps control computation, but learned methods can struggle when those subproblems have structures unlike their training examples. Generative Large Neighborhood Search addresses the choice of which part of a solution should undergo local repair.

The method uses a discrete diffusion model to generate neighborhoods. Its key signal comes from the denoising trajectory: variables whose predictions change substantially across steps identify regions where repair can lead to further improvements. A localized sampling procedure uses this instability signal to construct influential neighborhoods while bounding computational complexity, supporting neighborhood selection without retraining.

The reported experiments show transfer across cost structures and instance scales within set cover. Under equally tight wall-clock budgets, the method consistently beats established neural baselines and performs competitively with leading mixed-integer programming solvers. These results support trajectory-guided neighborhood selection for large set cover problems; the authors also suggest possible relevance to other constrained optimization tasks.
icml-2026-generative-large-neighborhood-.tldr: GLNS uses instability along diffusion denoising trajectories to select promising regions for scalable local repair in set cover optimization.

paragraphs: Language models may struggle with heterogeneous training material and subtle changes in the conditions they must follow. Fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting, while meta-learning approaches face complexity and scaling challenges. This paper introduces a mechanism that lets textual conditions directly influence part of the model’s internal computation, providing a targeted way to adapt its behavior.

The mechanism acts on a parameter called beta inside SwiGLU blocks. Changing beta adjusts the nonlinearity of the model’s feed-forward network. A hypernetwork produces these beta values from the textual condition, so the supplied text controls the gating behavior. This gives the model an internal adaptation mechanism tied to the condition it receives.

The authors test conditions describing tasks, domains, personas, and styles. Their method outperforms fine-tuning and meta-learning baselines in these evaluations and generalizes reasonably to unseen tasks, condition types, or instructions. The findings support text-conditioned control of feed-forward nonlinearities as a useful adaptation strategy, with the reported transfer extending beyond the particular conditions encountered during training.
icml-2026-learn-to-learn-on-arbitrary-te.tldr: A hypernetwork turns textual conditions into internal gating adjustments, improving adaptation across tasks, domains, personas, and styles.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text by repeatedly deciding which masked tokens to reveal. This sampling procedure affects both output quality and token throughput. Confidence-based heuristics can improve on random unmasking, but they require manual tuning, and the authors observe that their performance worsens as generation blocks become larger.

The paper learns the unmasking procedure with reinforcement learning. It describes sampling as a Markov decision process, treating the diffusion language model as the environment. A lightweight controller consisting of a single transformer layer receives token confidence scores and decides which tokens to unmask. This makes the generation schedule itself a learned policy instead of a manually specified rule.

In experiments using semi-autoregressive block generation, the learned policies match state-of-the-art heuristics. In full-diffusion generation, they outperform those heuristics. The distinction matters: the reported advantage depends on the generation setting. The results show that a compact learned controller can successfully manage unmasking decisions, with particular benefits when generation uses the full-diffusion setting.
icml-2026-learning-unmasking-policies-fo.tldr: Reinforcement learning trains compact unmasking controllers that match leading block-generation heuristics and outperform them in full-diffusion generation.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization contains one optimization problem inside another. This paper studies the smooth setting where the upper-level problem is nonconvex and the lower-level problem is strongly convex. It asks how much first-order information algorithms must obtain in difficult cases, complementing upper bounds that describe how quickly particular algorithms can succeed.

The authors construct hard instances for deterministic and stochastic first-order oracle models. In the deterministic case, any first-order zero-respecting algorithm requires at least Ω(κ^(3/2) ε^(-2)) oracle calls to reach an ε-accurate stationary point. In the stochastic case, they establish a lower bound of Ω(κ^(5/2) ε^(-4)) calls. These results concern stationarity rather than finding a global optimum.

The bounds strengthen known lower bounds in related single-level nonconvex and nonconvex–strongly-convex min-max settings. They also reveal substantial remaining gaps between available upper and lower bounds for bilevel optimization. The authors highlight even quadratic lower-level objectives as deserving further investigation, indicating that the best achievable complexity remains unresolved despite the new impossibility results.
icml-2026-lower-complexity-bounds-for-no.tldr: New hard instances establish stronger first-order complexity lower bounds for smooth nonconvex–strongly-convex bilevel optimization.

paragraphs: Multi-agent language systems can specialize agents through lightweight LoRA adapters while sharing a pretrained backbone. Yet each agent may still build a separate attention cache for the same long interaction history. LRAgent targets this duplicated storage and computation, using the observation that backbone activations remain highly similar while adapter outputs dominate differences between agents.

The framework separates the cache into a shared backbone component and an adapter-dependent component stored in low-rank form. With shared-A multi-LoRA architectures, it can also share the low-rank cache and reuse computation for contexts another agent has processed. Its Flash-LoRA-Attention kernel reorders attention operations so adapter contributions need not be expanded into a full-dimensional cache.

On agentic question-answering benchmarks, LRAgent achieves throughput and time-to-first-token latency close to fully shared caching, while maintaining accuracy near the separate-cache baseline. The results show that exploiting the structure of adapter differences can recover much of sharing’s efficiency while retaining agent specialization. The additional low-rank sharing benefits specifically rely on the stated shared-A architecture.
icml-2026-lragent-efficient-kv-cache-sha.tldr: LRAgent shares backbone and structured adapter caches to reduce multi-LoRA agent overhead while preserving accuracy near separate caching.

paragraphs: Brain-to-text interfaces are motivated by patients who cannot provide extensive training recordings. Pretraining across subjects can reduce the data needed for a new decoding task, but what it learns depends on how much temporal context it sees. MEG-XL investigates whether longer recordings provide useful statistical structure that short training windows discard.

The model is pretrained with 2.5 minutes of MEG context per sample, equivalent to 191,000 tokens. This is five to 300 times longer than the contexts used in prior work. The approach therefore exposes pretraining to extended neural activity, matching the observation that natural speech can unfold over minutes rather than only a few seconds.

When fine-tuned for word decoding from brain data, MEG-XL matches supervised performance using substantially less data, with an example of one hour versus 50 hours, and outperforms brain foundation models. The authors also find better transfer from models pretrained on longer contexts. These results support context length as an important ingredient in data-efficient neural representation learning for word decoding.
icml-2026-meg-xl-data-efficient-brain-to.tldr: MEG-XL uses minutes of neural context during pretraining to improve word decoding with substantially less fine-tuning data.

paragraphs: Agents that reason over long interaction histories need to locate relevant memories. A fixed retrieve-then-reason pipeline commits to its memory selection before later reasoning reveals what else matters. MRAgent instead makes memory access an active part of inference, allowing intermediate evidence to change which information the agent explores next.

The framework stores memories in a Cue–Tag–Content graph. Fine-grained cues connect to memory contents through associative tags that act as semantic bridges. During inference, the language model repeatedly explores and prunes paths through this structure using accumulated evidence. Pruning is central to the design because unrestricted graph expansion would create a combinatorial growth in possible retrieval paths.

On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, MRAgent reports improvements of up to 23% over strong baselines while substantially reducing retrieval cost. The findings support combining associative memory structure with adaptive exploration, rather than treating memory access as a fixed preliminary step. In these evaluations, reasoning-guided selection improves both the usefulness of retrieved information and the efficiency of obtaining it.
icml-2026-memory-is-reconstructed-not-re.tldr: MRAgent improves long-history reasoning by iteratively exploring and pruning an associative memory graph as evidence accumulates.

paragraphs: Conjoint experiments collect preferences over alternatives assembled from multiple attributes. Standard summaries average over an opponent’s attributes, potentially overlooking strategic interaction. This paper learns interpretable policies from randomized preference data, representing a policy as separate categorical distributions over attribute levels. This factorization makes choices manageable even when the number of possible combinations is exponential.

The approach supports both average-case outcome optimization and a two-player minimax setting in which competing sides choose strategically. The authors derive a closed-form optimizer for a tractable two-way interaction model with L2 variance regularization, alongside a gradient-based method for richer models. Under regularity conditions, a Delta method approximation propagates outcome-model uncertainty to the learned policy and its value.

The framework also incorporates institutional features such as primaries and measures strategic divergence between parties. Synthetic experiments examine finite-sample error and uncertainty coverage. In a U.S. presidential conjoint, adversarial policies produce restricted-equilibrium vote shares aligned with historical ranges in the studied data, unlike averaging-based optimizers. This illustrates how explicitly modeling an opponent changes the resulting policy estimates.
icml-2026-minimax-learning-of-interpreta.tldr: The paper learns interpretable strategic policies from conjoint preferences and quantifies their uncertainty under stated regularity conditions.

paragraphs: Generalist robot policies must work across different arms, grippers, tasks, and environments. Collecting demonstrations again for every embodiment is costly. This paper studies whether augmenting existing robot demonstrations can improve transfer, focusing on Open X-Embodiment. Although OXE combines over 60 datasets, four robot types account for more than 85% of its real data.

The authors introduce AugE-Toolkit and the OXE-AugE dataset, which augments OXE with nine different robot embodiments. The resulting collection contains over 4.4 million trajectories, more than three times the original dataset’s size. Their systematic study examines how increasing robot augmentation affects cross-embodiment learning, addressing both the amount of data and the diversity of arms and grippers represented.

Results suggest benefits for augmented robots, unseen robots, and original robots facing distribution shifts. In physical experiments across four manipulation tasks, fine-tuning generalist policies such as OpenVLA and π₀ improves success rates by a reported 24–45% on unseen robot–gripper combinations. These findings support augmentation as a way to improve embodiment transfer using existing demonstrations.
icml-2026-oxe-auge-a-large-scale-robot-a.tldr: OXE-AugE expands existing robot demonstrations across embodiments and improves transfer to unseen arm–gripper combinations in physical experiments.

paragraphs: EnergyFlow connects generating expert-like actions with recovering the rewards behind expert behavior. It represents a scalar energy function whose gradient provides the denoising field used for action modeling. This gives the generative policy an explicit mathematical structure that can also support inverse reinforcement learning, rather than learning action generation and reward extraction separately.

Under maximum-entropy optimality, the authors show that denoising score matching recovers the gradient of the expert’s soft Q-function. This enables reward extraction without adversarial training. They also prove that requiring a conservative field reduces hypothesis complexity and tightens out-of-distribution generalization bounds. Further analysis characterizes reward identifiability and bounds how score-estimation errors affect inferred action preferences.

Experiments report state-of-the-art imitation performance across manipulation tasks. The recovered reward also supports downstream reinforcement learning more effectively than adversarial inverse reinforcement learning methods and likelihood-based alternatives. Together, these findings connect the theoretical structure needed for valid reward extraction with a useful learning bias for policy generalization, while the reward-recovery result retains its maximum-entropy assumption.
icml-2026-recovering-hidden-reward-in-di.tldr: EnergyFlow structures diffusion action models to recover rewards under maximum-entropy optimality while improving imitation and downstream reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Federated learning can reduce computation by training on informative subsets of data. Existing coreset methods, however, may retain the same fraction of data at every client despite differences in client usefulness. ShapCCS moves selection to the client level, addressing the paper’s concern that uniform retention can leave fragmented clients with negligible or harmful contributions.

The method introduces a gradient projection Shapley value that uses both the direction and magnitude of client updates to assess contribution. It enables exact Shapley calculation with constant-time evaluation per coalition; that statement concerns each coalition evaluation, not the entire calculation. ShapCCS prioritizes clients with high scores and excludes fragmented clients whose scores are negligible or negative.

Client selection can be combined with data-level coreset construction, allowing both approaches to operate together. It also reduces communication costs, an advantage the authors distinguish from data-only selection. Experiments report superior model performance and robustness to noise. The findings support accounting for client heterogeneity when deciding which participants should represent the wider federated dataset.
icml-2026-shapccs-shapley-driven-client-.tldr: ShapCCS selects informative federated-learning clients using gradient-based Shapley contributions, reducing communication while improving reported performance and noise robustness.

paragraphs: Pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning appear to benefit from different kinds of data. This paper asks why scale and example difficulty matter differently across these stages. The authors analyze transformers on an in-context linear-regression weight-prediction task, providing a controlled setting for studying how post-training interacts with capabilities acquired earlier.

Their analysis finds that balanced pretraining data can create latent capabilities that post-training subsequently activates. Supervised fine-tuning works best with a small collection of examples that challenge the pretrained model. Excessively large fine-tuning datasets may dilute informative signals from pretraining. Reinforcement learning shows a different preference: large datasets whose examples are not overly difficult for the starting model.

The authors validate these theoretical insights through experiments with large nonlinear transformer architectures. The findings make data quality dependent on both the training stage and the model’s existing abilities. In the studied setting, challenging examples are valuable for supervised fine-tuning, while reinforcement learning benefits from broader experience at a manageable difficulty level; the analysis does not establish a universal dataset recipe.
icml-2026-theoretical-perspectives-on-da.tldr: Theory and experiments suggest supervised fine-tuning favors small, challenging datasets, while reinforcement learning benefits from larger datasets of manageable difficulty.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a small group of neurons plays an unusually important role across a language model’s capabilities. Across a wide range of open-weight transformers, the authors observe neurons that remain strongly activated on tasks spanning multiple capability dimensions. Probing this cross-task activation isolates an extremely sparse subset whose removal causes model behavior to collapse.

The authors call this subset keystone neurons. Their analysis indicates that these neurons form a stable, intrinsic part of the model and are largely established during pretraining. The associated parameters are tightly calibrated through training, with their precise values critical to model capabilities. The removal experiments connect the observed activation pattern to a consequential role in behavior.

Building on this finding, the paper proposes supervised fine-tuning that updates only keystone neurons. It achieves task improvements comparable to or better than full-parameter fine-tuning while preserving other capability dimensions more effectively. The results suggest that identifying this sparse subset can support targeted adaptation, changing far fewer parameters while retaining useful performance outside the fine-tuned task.
icml-2026-tiny-brains-giant-impact-uncov.tldr: A sparse set of highly active keystone neurons proves critical to model behavior and supports effective targeted fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Some questions about tables ask for answers that are not explicitly recorded. They require predicting unobserved outcomes from historical patterns, even when the wording does not directly request a prediction. TopBench evaluates this distinction, separating ordinary retrieval and aggregation from the harder combination of recognizing predictive intent and reasoning reliably over large tables.

The benchmark contains 779 samples across four subtasks: single-point prediction, decision making, treatment-effect analysis, and complex filtering. Expected outputs include both reasoning text and structured tables. The authors evaluate diverse models using text-based and agentic workflows, examining whether different ways of interacting with tabular data support these implicitly predictive requests.

The experiments find that models often misread intent and default to looking up existing values. Further analysis identifies correct intent disambiguation as a prerequisite for eliciting predictive behavior. It also finds that improving the upper bound of prediction precision requires stronger modeling or reasoning. The benchmark therefore exposes two connected challenges: deciding that prediction is needed and performing that prediction accurately.
icml-2026-topbench-a-benchmark-for-impli.tldr: TopBench tests whether models recognize and answer implicitly predictive table questions, revealing frequent confusion between prediction and lookup.

paragraphs: Generated code can look plausible while failing to perform its intended function. This paper addresses the difficulty of judging functional correctness by using code’s executable nature. Dynamic code analysis tools automatically generate unit tests, providing behavioral evidence that can inform both evaluation and the decision to return a generated program.

The proposed selective generator abstains when generated tests leave it uncertain about correctness. Its goal is theoretical control of the false discovery rate among the answers it does return. This focuses the guarantee on the collection of accepted outputs, rather than asserting that every generated program is correct. Abstention becomes part of how the system manages unreliable code generation.

The authors also propose FuzzEval, a paradigm that uses generated unit tests in both evaluation and learning to support more precise code assessment. Their results demonstrate the method’s efficacy, controllability of code hallucination, and reasonable selection efficiency. The contribution links executable testing with selective output, giving correctness evidence a direct role in deciding which answers reach users.
icml-2026-towards-functional-correctness.tldr: Automatically generated unit tests support selective code generation that abstains on uncertainty and theoretically controls false discoveries among accepted answers.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can struggle when visual problems require extended chains of reasoning. This paper attributes a central difficulty to visual information becoming diluted as generation grows longer. Vision-aligned Latent Reasoning addresses that problem by repeatedly supplying visually aligned internal representations as the model develops its reasoning, helping perceptual evidence remain available throughout the process.

Before each chain-of-thought step, VaLR dynamically generates latent tokens aligned with vision. Training aligns intermediate language-model embeddings with embeddings from vision encoders, encouraging preservation of visual knowledge during reasoning. The mechanism therefore operates inside the model’s representation space, using these latent tokens to guide successive reasoning steps with perceptual cues.

Across benchmarks requiring long-context understanding or precise visual perception, VaLR consistently outperforms existing approaches in the reported experiments. It also exhibits test-time scaling behavior that the authors did not observe in prior multimodal models. On VSI-Bench, performance rises from 33.0% to 52.9%, a 19.9-percentage-point gain over Qwen2.5-VL. The results support maintaining visual alignment as a useful ingredient in extended multimodal reasoning.
icml-2026-vision-aligned-latent-reasonin.tldr: VaLR inserts vision-aligned latent tokens before reasoning steps to preserve visual information and improve extended multimodal reasoning.

paragraphs: Visually convincing generated images can still contain the wrong objects, relationships, or counts. This paper investigates how training data contributes to such multi-object failures. The authors introduce mosaic, a controlled dataset-generation framework covering spatial relations, attribution, and counting, so they can vary data conditions and study their effects on diffusion models.

The study separates two regimes across different dataset sizes. Concept generalization includes every individual concept during training but permits imbalanced frequencies. Compositional generalization systematically withholds particular combinations of concepts. This separation helps distinguish difficulty learning from uneven concept exposure from difficulty assembling familiar concepts into combinations absent from the training data.

In the controlled experiments, scene complexity plays a more dominant role than concept imbalance, while counting is especially difficult when data is scarce. Compositional generalization collapses as more combinations are withheld. These findings point to substantial weaknesses in the studied models’ multi-object generation and motivate stronger inductive biases and more deliberate data design. They also show why balancing individual concepts alone may not address the central difficulties.
icml-2026-when-do-diffusion-models-learn.tldr: Controlled experiments identify scene complexity, low-data counting, and withheld concept combinations as major obstacles to multi-object diffusion generation.
